title: AI Service Failing in Production (Cloud / Platform)

teaser.setup: You're on call for the platform running a customer-facing AI service (any cloud). At 9am it's slow, error rates climb, and the bill is trending up. Run the incident and defend every move.
you_will_practice: Latency spikes, provider outages, and autoscaling

sample_node.prompt: You confirm the model provider itself is degraded/down. What protects the service?
sample_node.model: Timeouts + retries with backoff (bounded, with jitter) so you fail fast, not pile up; a circuit breaker that trips to a fallback (alternate provider/region or a smaller model) via your gateway; graceful degradation — cached/partial answers or a clear 'try again' rather than hanging. You don't control the provider; you control your blast radius. Communicate status to customers.

n1.prompt: The alert fires: latency up, errors climbing, cost trending up. What's your first move?
n1.model: Stabilize + scope before fixing. Acknowledge the incident, check the dashboards for the blast radius (which service/region/tenant, since when), and look for a recent change (deploy, config, provider status, traffic spike). Don't shotgun fixes. Establish a single hypothesis and a comms channel. Mitigate first (protect users), root-cause second.

n2.prompt: Nothing obvious deployed. How do you isolate which layer is failing?
n2.model: Bisect the request path with your traces/metrics: gateway/auth → retrieval/data → model provider → post-processing. Look at per-hop latency and error rate to find the slow/failing hop. Check the cheap things first: expired credentials, a dependency's status page, rate limits, a config/env change, a saturated resource (CPU/mem/connections). One hypothesis, test it, narrate.
signals: bisect the request path with traces
per-hop latency to find the hop

n3.prompt: You confirm the model provider is degraded. What protects the service?
n3.model: Timeouts + bounded retries with backoff/jitter so you fail fast, not pile up; a circuit breaker tripping to a fallback (alternate provider/region or smaller model) via the gateway; graceful degradation — cached/partial answers or a clear retry, not hanging. You don't control the provider; you control your blast radius. Post customer status.

n4.prompt: Turns out it's peak-hour load, not the provider — requests are queuing. What do you change?
n4.model: Scale the stateless tier horizontally (autoscaling on the right signal — queue depth / concurrency, not just CPU); add backpressure + a concurrency cap so slow calls don't exhaust workers; shed or queue non-interactive load; route easy requests to a smaller/faster model on the hot path; cache hot results. The model/provider is usually the throughput bottleneck — size and route accordingly. Fix the autoscaling signal so it pre-empts next peak.

n5.prompt: Meanwhile cost has spiked hard. Find and stop it without breaking the service.
n5.model: Attribute the spike by workload/tenant/model from cost telemetry — don't guess. Usual culprits: a retry storm hammering an expensive model, an agent stuck looping, or a batch job with no pre-filter. Stop the bleed: cap retries, add loop/step limits, pre-filter before inference, route to a cheaper model, throttle the offending workload. Then add a budget alert + per-request cost metric so it's caught before the invoice.

n6.prompt: Root cause: a config change did ship 20 minutes ago via an untracked path. What now?
n6.model: Roll back to the last known-good immediately (mitigate first) — don't debug forward under fire. Confirm recovery on the dashboards. Then: how did an untracked change reach prod? Enforce change through CI/CD with review, canary + automatic rollback on SLO regression, and config-as-code so every change is versioned and revertible. A fast, clean rollback path is the point.

n7.prompt: The interviewer asks: how do you keep one failure from taking down everything next time?
n7.model: Contain blast radius by design: isolate tenants/workloads (quotas, separate queues/capacity for batch vs interactive), bulkheads + circuit breakers between dependencies, multi-AZ and a tested failover, and SLOs with alerting so you detect early. Degrade gracefully rather than cascade. Test failure (game-days/chaos), don't assume it. Blast-radius control is a design property, not a runbook line.

n8.prompt: What observability did you need to run this incident — and what will you add?
n8.model: You needed end-to-end tracing (per-hop latency), error rates + saturation per dependency, per-request/per-tenant cost, and a change log correlated to metrics. Add what was missing: SLOs + burn-rate alerts, a status page, cost anomaly alerts, and dashboards that show blast radius fast. You can't fix fast what you can't see — observability is what turned this from guessing into bisecting.

n9.prompt: Where did you jump to a fix instead of stabilizing, scoping, and isolating first?
checklist: I isolated the failing layer with traces, not guesses
I protected against the provider with breakers + fallback
I autoscaled on the right signal under load
I attributed and stopped the cost spike
I rolled back first, then closed the change-control gap
I designed for blast-radius containment + observability

n10.prompt: Well handled. Push into more incidents and design:

recommend.label: Keep Asking Why — cost / reliability chains
